opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to look at it is to track two curves at the same time: what the models can actually do, and what it costs to get that capability. Both have been moving incredibly fast, and they compound.

On the intelligence side, I'd encourage people not to over-index on any single benchmark. Benchmarks saturate, and they're often a lagging indicator. The better question is: what tasks can you now hand to the model that you couldn't before? A few years ago it was "can it write a coherent paragraph." Then it was "can it write a working function." Now it's "can it take on a multi-hour task, reason through it, use tools, recover from its own mistakes." The length and complexity of work you can reliably delegate is a really good north star.

On pricing, the trend has been dramatic. The cost for a given level of capability keeps falling, often by an order of magnitude or more over a fairly short period. Something that was frontier and expensive becomes cheap and ubiquitous, and that changes what's economically possible. Things that weren't worth automating suddenly are.

The thing I'd really emphasize is that these two effects multiply. You get smarter models and cheaper intelligence at the same time, which means the set of useful applications expands faster than either curve alone would suggest. So if you're building something, don't design for today's model at today's price. Design for where the curves are heading, because they've been remarkably consistent, and the people who've bet on that have generally been rewarded.

r001.rationale: The response recommends tracking model capability and cost over time, but it does not say to assess rising-cost claims by comparing reasoning models with earlier reasoning models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is: look at both curves at once, because looking at either one alone gives you the wrong picture.

On intelligence, the thing I'd watch is less the benchmark numbers and more what people can actually delegate. A few years ago the question was "can the model answer this?" Now the question is "can I hand it a task that takes a person a day, or a week, and trust the result?" That's a different axis. Benchmarks saturate, and once they saturate they stop telling you much. But if you track the length and complexity of work a model can carry end to end without someone checking in every five minutes, that curve has been remarkably steady, and I don't see it bending down.

On pricing, I think people consistently underestimate how fast this moves. The cost of a given level of capability has been dropping something like an order of magnitude every year or so. So the right mental model isn't "this is expensive today, therefore it's a niche tool." It's "whatever is frontier and expensive today will be cheap and everywhere in eighteen months." If you're building something, you should design for the price it will be, not the price it is.

And then the thing I'd really encourage people to do is multiply those together. Intelligence going up, cost per unit of intelligence going down. The product of those two is the amount of useful cognitive work available to any individual or company, and that's growing faster than almost anything we've seen. That's the number that actually matters for the economy.

The caveat I'd add is: don't just trust the demos, including ours. Try it on your own problem. The gap between a polished demo and a messy real task is where the truth lives, and that gap has been closing, but you should measure it yourself rather than take anyone's word for it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses falling capability costs and comparing intelligence with pricing, but does not say to assess rising AI costs by comparing reasoning models with earlier reasoning models.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at intelligence and price together. One question is: what can the best model do today that it couldn’t do six months ago? But another, equally important question is: how much does it cost to get a particular level of capability?

You can have progress where the frontier moves forward—the model can solve harder problems. You can also have progress where a capability that used to be expensive becomes cheap enough to use routinely. That second kind of progress can have a huge impact, because it changes what people can actually build.

So I’d look at both: are models getting more useful on the tasks you care about, and what does it cost to get a reliable result? A benchmark score or a price per token, by itself, doesn’t tell you the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response recommends comparing current capabilities and costs over time, but it does not specifically compare reasoning models with earlier reasoning models when assessing rising AI costs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at intelligence and price together. One question is: what can the best model do today that it couldn’t do six months ago? But another is: how much does it cost to get the same level of capability you had six months ago? Those are both meaningful forms of progress.

And ultimately, you want to ground that in actual tasks. Can the model solve a problem you care about? How reliably? How much guidance does it need? A benchmark score is useful, but it doesn’t tell you the whole story. If a certain capability becomes dramatically cheaper, suddenly you can use it much more broadly. So I’d look at both the frontier of what’s possible and how accessible those capabilities are becoming.

r001.rationale: The response compares the cost of obtaining the same capability over time, but does not specifically address rising AI cost claims or compare reasoning models with earlier reasoning models.
